title: Built For a Smell
aliases: A Town That Lasts One Day
logline: A walled town on a rock headland with the sea on three sides, fortified by one European trading company and then rebuilt over sixty years by another, because of what the bark of one tree tastes and smells like — and the wall they built is also the warehouse, so the wanting and the container for it are the same masonry.
human_question: If everything I want were built out of stone instead of felt, would there be anything warm in it at all?

place.what_kind_of_place: An inhabited walled town on a low rock headland, with open sea on three sides and a bay on the fourth. Inside a continuous circuit of earth-backed stone ramparts — coral blocks and granite, with arrowhead and half-moon bastions at the angles — there is a grid of narrow streets, two-storey houses with shuttered verandahs, a mosque, churches, a temple, courts, a library, a nineteenth-century clock tower, a lighthouse on the seaward corner, and warehouses, one of which is built bodily into the thickness of the wall with a gate driven through the middle of it. It is a World Heritage site and at the same time an ordinary residential street plan where about a thousand people live, with the number falling and most of the buildings now turned over to the visitor trade. It is not a military work with a town inside it; it is a town whose outer wall happens to be a fortification, and the wall is walkable all the way round.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things, none of them aerial and none of them at golden hour. First, hard high coastal light on burnt-white coral: a rampart in overhead sun is almost colourless, salt blooming in the joints, the sea beyond it flat and glaring, and the only black in the frame is the shadow inside a gate passage. Second, the object the whole film turns on is a single arch that can be filmed from both sides in one move — a gate pierced through a two-storey warehouse that is itself inside the wall, carrying one empire's arms on the face that looks at the water and the earlier company's arms, with its cockerel and a date in Roman numerals, on the face that looks into the town. Third, the interior of the wall: vaulted, thick-walled rooms where the air is measurably cooler than the street, which is what they were for. Around all of it a town is going about a Tuesday at street level, and the sea is on three sides of everything.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Water, heat and traffic through one opening. The swell works three sides of the headland and the tide changes what the wall foot looks like. Salt dries white on stone through the day. The shadow in the gate passage narrows to almost nothing at noon and then opens again. Vehicles, handcarts, animals and people pass through the arch continuously, so the one static object in the film is the only thing that does not move. Nothing in it needs a crew's intervention and nothing is scheduled; the film has no event in it at all, which is deliberate.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry months on this coast, roughly December to March, in the hard hours either side of noon — the opposite of what a fort is usually filmed in. High sun is what bleaches the coral, kills the modelling in the wall and makes the gate passage read as a hole rather than a surface, and it is what keeps this film from becoming a study of masonry texture. A calm sea helps the rampart circuit; a rough one helps the seaward bastion. The vaulted interiors want the middle of the day, when the outside is at its brightest and the difference in the doorway is largest.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A town film, walked. Start outside at the foot of a sea wall in glaring light, go up onto the rampart and follow the circuit, find the warehouse built into the wall and go into its cool vaulted rooms, come out through the arch onto the harbour side, turn and look back at it, then drop down into the streets and come back up onto the wall where you started. It has a complete shape of its own: outside, inside, through, and round. Nothing is staged, there is no event, and the payoff is a cut — the two faces of one arch, back to back.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes an inventory of wanting with no person in it, which is the only honest way to film this group's concepts. The voice never says what anybody is feeling; it reads objects. The bark two companies fortified a headland for. The room inside the wall where it was kept cool. The arms carved on two sides of one gate. The registers of a department that took delivery without paying. And it lands the sources' own reversal, which is the film's argument: they rank flat, unexcited wanting above the glad kind, and a fort is what flat wanting looks like when somebody builds it out of coral. The film also says out loud what it cannot do — a lens cannot find which of the eight kinds of wanting is in anybody — so the burden stays on the wall and never moves onto a face.

sequence.on_screen: Hard mid-morning light. Ground level, outside the walls, walking the foot of a rampart on a rock headland: coral blocks and granite courses, salt bloom in the joints, the sea flat and glaring beyond. No people in frame, no drone, no move that a person could not make on foot.
sequence.voice: Two chartered trading companies fortified this headland, one after the other, and the second of them spent about sixty years making the wall you are walking beside. They did it for the bark of a tree. Not the wood, not the fruit, not the timber — the bark, and specifically what it tastes of and what it smells of. Chemists put the aldehyde that carries that smell at between sixty-five and eighty per cent of the oil in it. That is what this is for. The books this series is about start their account of ordinary life with the mind that lives among things seen, heard, smelled, tasted and touched, and they count fifty-four kinds of moment in it.

sequence.on_screen: Up onto the rampart top and walking it at an even pace: the circuit running away in both directions, the angle of a bastion, the roofs of an inhabited town inside and open sea outside. Sun almost overhead, shadows short and hard.
sequence.voice: These books have a term for the flavour of an object — its taste, whether the object is a sound, a thought or a piece of bark. Feeling, in their account, is nothing more than the tasting of that flavour, and since every mind takes an object, every mind has one. It can go three ways: agreeable, disagreeable, or neither, and they say flatly that there is no fourth way. Sixty-two kinds of mind are counted glad, fifty-five flat. Everything built on this headland was arranged around one flavour.

sequence.on_screen: The warehouse: two storeys of it built into the thickness of the rampart, wall and store the same masonry, with the gate driven through the middle. Then inside — vaulted rooms, walls a metre and more thick, bare floors, the air visibly different in the doorway.
sequence.voice: The wall is also the warehouse. Part of this building sits inside the thickness of the rampart, which is not how this company built elsewhere. The cool rooms low down took the bark, and cardamom, and cloves. The dry rooms above took gems, pearls, silk, porcelain and ivory. Sight, smell, taste and touch, sorted by floor and stored by temperature. A camera can film every object on that list. It cannot film one single wanting, and that is not a limitation of the camera.

sequence.on_screen: Out through the arch to the harbour side, then turn and look back at it. The outer face: a crown held by a lion and a unicorn, a motto in French. Cut, hard, to the inner face of the same arch: two lions holding a monogram, a cockerel above it, the year in Roman numerals.
sequence.voice: One arch, two faces, two coats of arms. The company's own, with its cockerel, was cut into this in sixteen sixty-nine. When the next empire took the place it moved that one round to the inside and put its own crown on the face that looks at the water. The books sort wanting on three dials, and the second is whether it arrives with a story attached. Their own examples of the story are denials of consequence and excuses that happen to suit the person making them — the rich have plenty, it was ill-gotten anyway, the gods gave it to us. Both faces of this arch are a claim of right, carved in stone at public expense. This film reads what is carved and passes sentence on nobody.

sequence.on_screen: Static, long, no camera move. The gate passage seen from inside: the full depth of the wall as a dark tunnel with white light at the far end, people and a handcart crossing it as silhouettes. Then, held, an eighteenth-century engraved plan of the place, its bastions lettered against a key.
sequence.voice: The bark was cut and peeled inland and brought down to this store. It came without payment, in fixed quantities, under a hereditary obligation that a great cinnamon department's own registers attached to a single caste. The penalties for falling short are written down in the company's papers. Nothing written by the people under that obligation was found in researching this film. The books make a distinction here that is worth keeping exactly as they make it: they separate the suffering anyone can see — violence, confinement, things done in the open — from the kind that cannot be known at all unless somebody asks. There is no record of anyone asking.

sequence.on_screen: The sheer mass of the thing in overhead sun: the batter of a bastion from directly below, courses going up out of frame, heat shimmer coming off white coral. Nothing moves anywhere in the frame except a little sea at the very bottom.
sequence.voice: The third dial is whether the wanting came up by itself or had to be urged along — by somebody else, or by talking a part of yourself that was holding back into going ahead. Neither of these companies wanted this bark of its own accord. Both were pushed: by a market on the far side of the world, by what the bark fetched there, and by each other. And the books say something about the urged kind that nothing else here can match. It carries a heaviness. A sluggishness, in their words, which the sharp spontaneous kind does not have — and heaviness is the one property of all this that a camera can actually photograph.

sequence.on_screen: The lighthouse on the seaward bastion in flat glare, and past it the roadstead: open water with nothing anchored in it. Then the jubilee clock tower on the landward wall, its face reading the ordinary time of an ordinary afternoon.
sequence.voice: On the tenth of June, seventeen sixty, a great quantity of this same bark was destroyed beside the company's own admiralty back home, to stop the price falling, and as much again the following day. Nobody was glad about that. It was arithmetic. One of these two books ranks flat, unexcited wanting as stronger than the joyful kind, and stronger again when a justification comes with it — so on that reckoning the cold version outweighs the giddy one. Its own compilers note that the passage gives no commentarial ground for the ranking and that it needs checking, so this film does not lean on the weight. It only observes that if you had to build flat wanting out of something, it would come out looking like this.

sequence.on_screen: Down off the wall and into the streets at walking pace: a grid of lanes, shutters, salt-marked plaster, an animal standing in a crossroads, a minaret and a church tower over the roofline, the sea showing at the end of a street. Then back up the steps onto the rampart and the circuit closing where it began.
sequence.voice: The bark is an ordinary garden tree now, and the harbour lost its shipping to a built one along the coast a century and a half ago. About a thousand people still live inside these walls; a generation ago it was nearly three thousand, and most of the buildings have gone over to the visitor trade. So the thing wanted here now is the walls. One last thing the books are careful about, and it is why this film has stayed off faces: no camera can show which of the eight kinds of wanting is present in a person, or whether any of them is. And of the fifty-four moments they count in ordinary sense life, twenty-four are classed as beautiful. So none of this is a verdict on wanting, and none of it is a verdict on anybody living in this street.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the three digests do three separate jobs and this place needs all three. C006 is the anatomy: the same wanting sorted on three dials — glad on meeting a pleasing object or flat on meeting a neutral one [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74], with a justifying story or without one [C006-P:L33], and arising sharply of its own nature or having to be urged along by somebody else or by pushing a hesitating mind of one's own [C006-P:L44] [C006-M:L5] [C006-P:L58–L62]. C004 supplies the world those dials turn in and the definition of the thing being measured: the sense-sphere mind that lives among sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches [C004-P:L25], with greed defined as the attaching that takes a thing to be good, beautiful or sweet [C004-M:L13], which is what a spice literally is, and attaching that fastens on a pleasing or a neutral object and never on a disagreeable one [C004-P:L41] [C004-M:L15]. C032 supplies the object's other half. Its whole subject is ārammaṇa-rasa, the flavour of an object, and feeling as the bare tasting of that flavour, present in every mind because every mind takes an object [C032-P:L41] [C032-P:L43], going three ways and no fourth [C032-M:L5]. Put on this headland the three of them stop being a taxonomy, because here the object of a century and a half of wanting actually was a flavour — a bark valued for nothing but its taste and its smell — and the wanting was built, in coral and granite, at the scale of a town. The dials can be read off the object rather than off a person: the axis of the justifying story is carved on two faces of one gate arch, the axis of urging is the reason two companies came at all, and the heaviness the sources attribute to the urged kind is the only attribute of this whole apparatus that a lens can register.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the sources' most counter-intuitive claim is the one a building can demonstrate. The Margaya ranks the flat, unexcited greed-rooted mind as stronger than the glad one, and the view-backed as stronger than the view-free [C006-M:L19], and there is no way to film that on a face — gladness photographs, flatness does not, and either way the digests forbid reading a mental factor off anybody. A fortified commodity town can do it. There is no gladness anywhere in a rampart, a quota register or an ordinance against private dealing; those are the cold, administered, justified form of the same wanting the books say is the heavier one, and the film can lay the whole of it out in daylight without a single person in frame carrying it. C032 then stops the film from becoming a sermon about appetite, because it keeps the flavour where the sources put it — in the tasting, not in the bark — and its counts show flat feeling running through fifty-five kinds of mind including the most refined ones [C032-P:L75–L83], so flat is not a synonym for cold-blooded and the film cannot use it as one. And C004 closes the exit that would wreck it: twenty-four of the fifty-four sense-sphere minds are counted beautiful [C004-P:L27], so these books do not treat a life of smells and tastes as a trap, and a film about a commodity must not leave a viewer thinking it has just been told that wanting things is wicked. The pairing also keeps the history honest. The one thing the record cannot be used for is a verdict, and the sources agree: the axis of the justifying story is about denying consequences, not about grading anybody's cause [C006-P:L33], and the strength ranking that makes this film's argument is flagged by our own digest as needing an expert check [C006-M:L19].

concept_links.why: The film is this digest's three axes performed by one object. Wanting arises glad when the object met is pleasing [C006-P:L25] and flat when the object is neither pleasing nor displeasing [C006-P:L74]; it comes with a justifying view or without one, and the views in question are denials of consequence and self-serving excuses such as the rich having plenty, wealth being ill-gotten anyway, or the gods having given it [C006-P:L33] [C006-M:L3]; and it either rises sharply of its own nature or has to be urged, by another person or by one's own pushing of a mind that is holding back [C006-P:L44] [C006-M:L5] [C006-P:L58–L62]. A commodity fortification puts each of those where a camera can reach it — the second on two faces of one arch, the third in the plain fact that a market on another continent is what brought both companies — and the digest's note that the urged kind carries a heaviness the spontaneous kind does not [C006-P:L62] gives the film the only visual property it needs. The digest's limits are written into the beats and not parked in the risks. The strength ranking that the film's argument rests on [C006-M:L19] is recorded in the digest as having no commentarial basis in the extract and needing an expert check, so beat 7 states the ranking, names the doubt and declines to lean on it. 'Wrong view' must never be mapped onto any community's faith, so the film reads two coats of arms and passes no sentence; it does not adjudicate a colonial claim of right, and it does not narrate anybody's grievance or anybody's due. 'I was pushed into it' is not an excuse in these sources — prompted wanting is ranked weaker and is still wanting — so beat 6 says the companies were pushed and does not thereby excuse anything. The background conditions the Pradeepika lists for the spontaneous kind, including the rebirth-mind, temperament, health, patience, habit, company, and suitable weather and food [C006-P:L46–L52], describe tendencies and not fate and are not read onto anyone, living or dead. And the three courses of action the digest says are done only through greed [C006-P:L54] are not laid against any named historical person: no individual in this history is classified.

This is the world the count is a count of, and it is unusually literal here. Sense-sphere minds are the minds of the world of sight, sound, smell, taste and touch [C004-P:L25]; the Margaya's definition of greed is the attaching that takes a thing to be good, beautiful or sweet [C004-M:L13], and the object at the centre of this film is a bark whose entire value is that it is sweet; greed fastens on a pleasing or a neutral object and never comes with displeased feeling [C004-P:L41] [C004-M:L15]; and it divides by glad or flat and by spontaneous or prompted [C004-M:L17] [C004-M:L21], which is the same sorting the primary digest performs, so the two belong in one film rather than side by side. Beat 3's shot list is the sense-sphere count made into an inventory of storage: bark and cardamom in the cool rooms, gems, pearls, silk, porcelain and ivory in the dry rooms above. The digest's guard is the film's last beat and its whole posture: twenty-four of the fifty-four are counted beautiful [C004-P:L27], so these sources do not treat sense life as simply bad, and a film about a commodity must not leave a viewer with a moral about appetite. The Pradeepika's own contemporary commentary on meat, eggs, fishing, gambling, drink and other faiths' positions [C004-P:L55–L69] is that author's moral argument, is named in the digest as something that would wound if turned on people on screen, and is not carried here at all. Nor is the claim that delusion underlies every unwholesome mind [C004-P:L39] pointed at any historical actor; it is not in the voice, because on screen it would become an accusation of stupidity against named people.

This digest is what makes the title true and what keeps the film off the one register it must avoid. Feeling is the tasting of an object's flavour, present in every mind because every mind takes an object [C032-P:L41] [C032-P:L43], and it goes three ways with no fourth [C032-M:L5]; sixty-two minds carry gladness and fifty-five carry flat feeling [C032-M:L9] [C032-M:L13], with the four joyful greed-rooted minds sitting among the pleasant ones [C032-P:L58]. That is beat 2, and it is why the film can say a wall was built around a flavour without the sentence being a metaphor. Two of its guards are load-bearing. Neutral does not mean numb: fifty-five minds carry neutral feeling, including the most refined [C032-P:L75–L83], so the film may not turn flatness into a synonym for callousness, which is the obvious cheap move available to it. And the digest states outright that 'pleasant feeling is where wanting begins' is our own editorial compression rather than a sentence in either source — the extracts only place the joyful greed-rooted minds among the pleasant-feeling ones — so no beat asserts that causal link. Beat 5 uses the Pradeepika's distinction between open suffering, which anyone can see, and concealed suffering, which cannot be known unless somebody asks [C032-P:L119], exactly as the source frames it, to state what the archive does and does not contain. What the film does not do is put the further teaching to work: that all conditioned feeling counts as suffering [C032-P:L111] and that pleasant feeling becomes painful when it turns [C032-P:L117] would make a lost trade and a fallen port into a moral about impermanence, which is elegy and not this concept, and nothing in the sequence goes near it.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That wanting does not have to be hot to be serious, and that the version of it which gets built — surveyed, costed, walled, quota'd and written down — is the version with no warmth in it anywhere. The demonstration needs no belief and no person: a wall on a headland, a room inside the wall, and two coats of arms on one arch, all of it there because of what a bark tastes like. And, held against that, the plain admission that no camera and no viewer can tell from a face which kind of wanting is present, or whether any is.
what_must_be_real: The walls, the warehouse inside the wall, the two carved faces of the gate, the streets in use and the sea on three sides. Nothing is dressed, wetted, chalked, lit or cleaned; no carving is enhanced and no stone is moved. Nobody who lives inside the walls is a subject: residents, traders, visitors and staff appear only as they happen to pass, never held, never followed, never framed to look acquisitive, devout, prosperous or dispossessed, and no shot is built to make a resident an example of anything. No identifiable person is filmed inside a private house or courtyard. No worship in the mosque, the churches or the temple is filmed, interrupted or lit, and no religious building's interior is entered for a shot. No child is a character. The caste-bound obligation is stated once, factually, as the documents record it, with no caste characterised and no living community identified with it; the punishments are attributed to the company's own records and to the scholarship, never dramatised, never reconstructed, and no shot is composed to evoke them. The colonial history is recorded as layers and never adjudicated: no empire is praised, indicted or compared, and neither the fall of the port nor the fall in the resident population is narrated as anybody's due. The figures on population, ownership and building use are quoted as the study's figures with its date, or not quoted at all. The destruction of the 2004 tsunami is not filmed, referenced or alluded to in any beat.
position_hint: middle, late: the group's coldest and most architectural statement of what wanting is, best placed after at least one film has shown it warm and moving, so that a viewer already knows what is being withheld. It is also the group's clearest demonstration that the sources rank the flat kind above the glad one, which reverses the group's own working gloss, so it earns more if it lands after that gloss has been allowed to stand. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: The group's standing hazard: a camera cannot show greed, and no identifiable person may be framed as greedy, acquisitive, calculating or covetous in narration or in framing. This film's whole design is to move the wanting into masonry, carved arms and administrative records so that no face carries any of it; any cut that puts a resident, trader, visitor or official in the position of illustrating the doctrine breaks it.

Adjudicating the colonial history. The record here is layered — a Portuguese work, a company's rebuilding, a third empire's crown over the second's arms — and the film records the layers without ranking or sentencing them. The temptation is a knowing tone about empire; the digest's 'wrong view' axis is about denying consequences, not about grading anybody's cause, and one ironic line would turn a doctrinal film into an editorial.

The caste-bound workforce. It is stated once, flat, as the documents record it, and no caste is characterised, named in the voice, or associated with any living community or trade. The punishments reach us through the company's own papers and through recent scholarship reported in the press rather than from anyone subject to them, and the film says so rather than dramatising them.

Narrating the resident population's fall, the shift to the visitor trade or the foreign ownership share as decline, loss or a moral about tourism. Those are one researcher's figures with dates on them, and they are quoted as figures. Kamma is not fate: nothing about who lives inside these walls now or who does not may read as deserved, and no resident is invited to represent either side of it.

Duplicating IDEA-0009, which is the slate's other colonial fort in the same series and is an inventory of what a wall is made of, shot into dusk with macro work on an opened cross-section. This film may not argue from wall fabric, may not shoot macro on masonry, and may not shoot at dusk or golden hour. Its material claim is the opposite one: not what the wall is made of, but what it is for and what is inside it.

Duplicating IDEA-0096, the slate's cinnamon film, which is a peeling shed, a brass rod and a moment of yielding. Nothing here may be filmed in a peeling shed, on a plantation or at any stage of the craft; no stem, no knife, no quill, no drying rack. The bark appears in this film only as a stored commodity and as a word in the voice.

Drifting into a heritage travelogue. The town is extremely photographed and the ramparts at sunset are one of the most reproduced images in the country. The schedule's insistence on hard overhead light is a defence against that as much as a look.

The figures. The area, the bastion count, the export quantities, the annual revenue and every date attached to the lighthouse disagree between sources, and several of the most quoted numbers trace to a single unattributed page. Nothing conflicting is averaged, and nothing unverified is spoken in the voice as fact.

Filming inside the warehouse. The vaulted rooms are a state museum, and beat 3 — the wall opened as a room — depends on access that is a matter for the conserving authority, not a ticket. If it cannot be had, the film loses its middle.

Treating flat feeling as coldness or callousness. The C032 digest states that neutral feeling runs through fifty-five kinds of mind including the most refined, so 'flat' cannot be used as a synonym for heartless, which is the easiest wrong reading of this film's argument and the one the voice has to keep closing.
Letting the lost trade and the empty roadstead become an elegy about impermanence. That is a different concept and a worse film; the closing beat names what is wanted now instead.
drop_if: The interior of the warehouse built into the rampart cannot be filmed, and no other place on the site shows the wall as a container. That is the film's middle and its best single idea; without it this becomes a rampart film and the group already has enough walls.
Both faces of the gate arch cannot be filmed — for scaffolding, traffic, a closure or a permission — so the payoff cut does not exist. It is not stageable anywhere else.
The only way to film the inhabited streets is to make residents subjects, or filming at street level cannot be done without people being identifiable in a way they have not agreed to.
The conserving authority's conditions require the town to be shown as a heritage product, or any framing that the film cannot honestly give.

The caste-bound obligation turns out not to be establishable from the record at the level of certainty the voice states it at, in which case that beat goes rather than being softened into insinuation.

connections.note: The executed merge recorded here on 2026-09-25 is cleared. This record no longer holds the two-roadsides film, and the seasonal fruit roadside it had absorbed from IDEA-0021 is not carried anywhere: that material leaves the slate. IDEA-0021 has itself been rewritten onto a different place in another district and depends on nothing here, so nothing is orphaned by the clearing except the roadside film itself, which is gone. IDEA-0021's own connections entry still describes this record as having absorbed its previous film and is now stale; correcting it means editing another idea file and was not done.

The slate's other colonial fort film, in the first group, and the deliberate opposite piece of cinema. That one is an inventory of what a wall is made of — an opened cross-section, macro on coral, brick and reused carved granite, late raking light into dusk, and a name laid over an assemblage. This one never argues from fabric, never goes macro, never shoots at dusk, and is not about a wall at all: it is about a whole inhabited town, a commodity, and what the wall was built to contain.

The slate's third and fourth forts, in the third group: two works of one eighteenth-century war, filmed as pure designed geometry from directly above in flat noon, with substance refused. This film has no aerial geometry in it, is walked at ground and rampart level, and is about a town and a trade rather than a shape addressed to an enemy.

The slate's cinnamon film, in another group and another district: a smallholder peeling shed, a brass rod, a stem that will not give up its bark, and the mental factor of softness. It owns the plant and the craft entirely. This film owns the institution — the wall, the store, the monopoly and the department — and contains no peeling, no plantation and no stage of the craft.

The group's other film touching compulsory service under a state. That one is a lake made by forced labour to increase a palace's beauty, at first light, on water, with an atrocity stated once. This one is a commodity institution in hard noon on stone, and its labour fact is a delivery quota administered by a department. Both state the compulsion once and flat; neither dwells on it and neither adjudicates.

The group's other film in flat high daylight, so the distinction has to be held. That one is static, empty, silent and small — carved stone a hand's width across, no movement, a duration. This one moves continuously at walking pace, is inhabited, has traffic through it and the sea on three sides, and its payoff is a cut between two carved faces rather than a single held riser.

The slate's other coral film and the other film in this district: a mined reef, lime kilns and inland pits, where coral taken from the sea now stands in the plaster of houses. This film's coral is already in a wall and is never the subject; nothing here is about extraction, the reef or lime.

selection.reason: The group's only colonial film, its only walled town, its only film with a written commodity institution behind it, and its coldest treatment. It carries the group's primary concept on an object rather than on a person, which is what the group's hazard requires, and it is the only film on the slate that can demonstrate the sources' ranking of flat wanting above glad wanting without reading a mental state off a face. The merge with IDEA-0021 recorded here on 2026-09-25 is cleared: the roadside material was a working analogy — verges where produce is pressed on people who had not meant to stop — and it carried the concept by resemblance rather than by history, which is the specific failure this pass exists to correct. That material leaves the slate rather than moving anywhere, and IDEA-0021 stands as its own film in another district.

review.note: Rewritten whole, so any earlier verdict no longer applies. The old film went because it was the group's clearest case of the problem this pass was called to fix: two roadside selling strips, filmed through a long lens, demonstrating the spontaneous-and-prompted axis by resemblance — the place happened to look like what the concept said, and there was no story on either road that asked the concept's question. It also rested on a merge that existed to make two near-duplicates into one, which is tidiness rather than doctrine, and on an origin story resting on a single newspaper feature that other press accounts contradicted. That merge is now cleared, selection.merged_with is empty, and the roadside material leaves the slate rather than being rehoused. The historical binding is this. A walled town on a rock headland was fortified by one European trading company in the sixteenth century and then rebuilt over roughly sixty years by a second, which took it in March 1640, ran the island's coast from it until it captured a better harbour up the coast in 1656, and held it as the island's principal port until the end of the eighteenth century — and the reason, in the company's own accounting, was the bark of one tree, valued for nothing but its taste and its smell. The concept is the eight greed-rooted minds sorted on three dials, and here every dial is legible in the object rather than in a person: the axis of the justifying story is carved on the two faces of a single gate arch, one empire's crown facing the water and the earlier company's arms with its cockerel and the date 1669 turned inward; the axis of urging is the plain fact that neither company wanted this bark of its own accord and both were pushed by a market on another continent; and the wall is also the warehouse, part of it built inside the rampart's own thickness, with the bark kept in the cool rooms below and gems, pearls, silk, porcelain and ivory in the dry rooms above, so that the wanting and the container for it are the same masonry. The film's argument is the sources' least intuitive claim: the Margaya ranks flat, unexcited wanting above glad wanting and view-backed above view-free, and a fortified commodity town is what the flat, administered, justified version looks like when somebody builds it — there is no gladness anywhere in a rampart or a quota register. The guards. IDEA-0009 is the slate's other colonial fort and is an inventory of wall fabric in raking dusk light with macro on an opened cross-section; this film shares none of it — no fabric argument, no macro, no dusk, hard overhead light throughout, and a whole inhabited town rather than a wall. IDEA-0096 is the slate's separate cinnamon film and owns the plant and the craft; nothing here is filmed in a peeling shed or on a plantation and no stage of the craft appears. On the group's hazard, no identifiable person carries any of the wanting: the burden sits on masonry, carved arms and records, no face is held, no resident or trader is framed as acquisitive, and the last beat says out loud that no camera can find which of the eight minds is present in anybody. The caste question is stated once and flat, as the documents record it, with no caste named in the voice and none characterised, and the research found that the row's premise needed correcting: the caste-bound obligation was not a Dutch creation, the peelers' own words are absent from the archive, and the film says so using the sources' own distinction between suffering anyone can see and suffering that cannot be known unless somebody asks. The colonial layers are recorded and never adjudicated, the 2004 tsunami is excluded from every beat, the fall in the resident population is quoted as one researcher's dated figures and never as decline or desert, and the strength ranking the film's argument rests on is stated together with our own digest's note that it needs an expert check. Corrections made to the brief's own notes are listed in research_note and the disputes are kept apart from the certainties in historical_thread; nine reference images were verified on Commons.

suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place available where the concept is the documented history of the object and not a resemblance to it, and where the object is a whole town rather than a monument. The primary digest sorts one wanting on three dials, and a commodity fortification carries all three without a person in frame: the axis of the justifying story is literally carved on the two faces of one gate arch, one empire's crown on the harbour side and the earlier company's arms with its cockerel and ANNO MDCLXIX turned inward; the axis of urging is the plain historical fact that neither company came for this bark of its own accord, both having been pushed by a market on the far side of the world and by each other; and the flat, unexcited version of wanting that the Margaya ranks above the glad kind is exactly what a rampart, a quota register and an ordinance against private dealing are. The object of all of it was a flavour, which is the supporting digests' own subject: a bark valued for nothing but taste and smell, kept in cool vaulted rooms built inside the thickness of the wall itself, with gems, pearls, silk, porcelain and ivory in the dry rooms above — the sense-sphere world sorted by floor and stored by temperature. And it films, in a register nothing else on the slate uses: hard overhead coastal light on bleached coral, a walkable circuit with sea on three sides, a town in ordinary use at street level, a black hole of a gate passage at noon, and a payoff that is a cut between two carved faces rather than a view.

historical_thread.story:
A low rock headland closes the west side of a bay on the island's south coast, and a walled town stands on it. The Portuguese made landfall on this coast in 1505 and used the harbour, but chose the place as a permanent post only in 1588, after Rajasinha I of Sitawaka drove them back on it; what they then built was slight — a work of palm and mud named Santa Cruz, later extended with a watchtower, three bastions and a fortalice covering the harbour. A separate account dates the first fortification here, the Zwart Bastion or Black Fort, to 1520, and another dates a Franciscan chapel to 1541; the dates do not agree and the Portuguese work was earth and palisade in any case.

The Dutch East India Company took the place in 1640. Modern accounts put the assault between 8 and 13 March, with Commodore Willem Jacobszoon Coster commanding, in alliance with Rajasinha II of Kandy; the Portuguese captain was Lourenço Ferreira de Brito. Figures for the force differ sharply between accounts — 2,500 men in one, 3,350 European troops with 24 ships and at least 27 shallops in another — and so do the Dutch dead, given as 450 in one place and as high as 1,350 in another. The Dutch national archive's own caption on a contemporary print of the capture dates it to 9 February 1640, against the 8–13 March of the modern accounts. One account states that the fortress commanded 282 villages holding the most fertile cinnamon lands in the south, which is the reason anybody was there.

From 1640 the Company ran its Ceylon administration from this town. That lasted until it took Colombo from the Portuguese in 1656 — some accounts say 1658 — after which the capital moved and this became one of two commandements under the governor at Colombo, while remaining the island's principal port. The fort that stands is not the fort that was captured. The Company judged the Portuguese earthworks unsafe and walled the whole peninsula: the main run of the walls is dated to 1663, the oldest gate was completed in 1669 with a two-storey warehouse above it built into the thickness of the rampart, and the sea wall was finished in 1729. Fourteen bastions are named in the usual list — Sun, Moon, Star, Zwart, Akersloot, Aurora, Point Utrecht, Triton, Neptune, Clippenburg, Flagrock, Aeolus, Fishmark and Commandment — though an eighteenth-century engraved plan in the Dutch archive keys a work called die Katz that is not in the modern list. The enclosed area is given almost everywhere as 52 hectares.

The commodity was cinnamon, and it was administered rather than traded. Before the Europeans, extraction was done through rajakariya, the system of unpaid service owed to the crown. Under colonial rule it was organised through a cinnamon department, the Mahabadda, headed by a Company officer known as the captain of cinnamon, which took delivery of fixed quantities without payment from men of the Salagama caste as an obligatory hereditary caste service, kept registers of them, and punished shortfall and absence. Who made that obligation caste-bound is not agreed: one account dates the department to 1597, in the Portuguese period, and says the Portuguese already took cinnamon as a tax from the same caste; a Sinhala chronicle is cited for an assignment as early as the reign of Sapumal Kumaraya in 1447–1480; and a recent scholarly essay states that it was the Dutch who changed the social division of labour by segregating the role and assigning it to that caste. What is not disputed is the machinery: unpaid quotas, registers, and laws closing the escape of marrying out of the caste. The monopoly was defended at the other end as well. A nineteenth-century compilation records that plants above a set number were destroyed, that prepared cinnamon was thrown into the sea or burnt, and that on 10 June 1760 an enormous quantity was destroyed beside the Admiralty at Amsterdam, valued at eight million livres, with as much again burnt the following day. From about 1769 the Company turned from wild cinnamon to cultivation, Governor Iman Willem Falck raising it from seed in his garden and his kinsman Cornelis de Cock laying out a large plantation at Maradana.

The British took the fort on 23 February 1796, a week after Colombo. The monopoly passed to the English East India Company and was not finally abolished until 1833 or 1834. The British built the first lighthouse in 1848, a cast-iron tower by Alexander Gordon, made by Robinson of Pimlico; a new main gate was cut through the north wall in 1873; and a clock tower went up for Queen Victoria's jubilee in 1883. The port's primacy ended with engineering elsewhere: an artificial harbour was built at Colombo from 1873, and by December 1882 the mail steamers had abandoned this roadstead for it. The old lighthouse burnt down and was replaced on the Point Utrecht bastion, though sources give the fire as 1934 and as July 1936 and the new tower as 1938, 1939 and 1940.

The town inside the walls was never emptied; people have lived in it continuously since the colonial period, and more than half of the residents are recorded as Moors. It was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1988 as the Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications, under criterion (iv), as an urban ensemble showing the interaction of European architecture and South Asian traditions from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries. Research by Uditha Jinadasa at Leiden, reported in 2020, gives the resident population as 2,703 in 1988 and 1,068 at the time of the study; residential buildings fell from 72 per cent in 1992 to 32 per cent in 2016 while commercial buildings rose from 17 to 35 per cent; 66 per cent of facades had been altered since 1988; and 16 per cent of the real estate was in foreign hands in 2016.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C006's three dials are not illustrated here, they are performed, and by the object rather than by anybody in it.

Take the second dial first, because it is the one actually carved. The sources separate wanting that comes with a justifying story from wanting that comes without one, and their examples of the story are denials of consequence and excuses that suit the person making them [C006-P:L33] [C006-M:L3]. One arch on this site carries two of those stories on its two faces: the Company's arms, two lions, a monogram and a cockerel with the year cut in Roman numerals as 1669, and, on the side that faces the water, a later crown held by a lion and a unicorn with a motto in French, placed there when the next empire moved the earlier arms round to the inside. A claim of right, in stone, at public expense, twice, on one opening. The film can cut between them in a single move without narrating a verdict on either, which is what the digest requires and also what the standing decisions require of a colonial site: layers recorded, never adjudicated.

The third dial is the reason anyone was here. The sources call wanting unprompted when it arises sharply of its own nature, with no urging, no encouragement, no pushing along [C006-P:L44], and prompted when another urges it or when a person works up a mind that is holding back [C006-M:L5] [C006-P:L58–L62]. Neither trading company wanted this bark for itself. Both were urged: by a market on another continent, by the price it fetched there, and by each other — which is documented in the plainest possible form, as a fortress said to command 282 villages of cinnamon land and a company that walled an entire peninsula to keep them. And then the digest supplies the one property this film can photograph. The prompted kind, the Pradeepika says, carries a heaviness, a sluggishness, which occurs only in the prompted unwholesome minds and which the sharp spontaneous kind does not have [C006-P:L62]. Heaviness is the whole visual argument of a rampart. The thing is four hundred metres of it, in coral, under a vertical sun, doing nothing.

The first dial is the film's actual claim, and it is the one that needs the history rather than the architecture. Wanting comes glad when the object met is pleasing and flat when the object is neither pleasing nor displeasing [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74], and the Margaya then ranks them against expectation: flat above glad, view-backed above view-free, unprompted above prompted [C006-M:L19]. There is no way to film that ranking on a person, and every digest in this group forbids trying. A commodity institution can carry it. Nothing in a delivery quota, a register of men, an ordinance against private dealing or a decision to burn eight million livres of prepared bark beside a company's own admiralty in order to hold a price is glad. It is arithmetic. If the sources are right that the cold version is the heavier one, then this headland is the heavier one built at the scale of a town — and the film can say so while also saying, as our own digest says, that the extract gives no commentarial basis for the ranking and that it needs an expert check.

C004 supplies the object and stops the film moralising. Greed, in the Margaya's definition, is the attaching that takes a thing to be good, beautiful or sweet [C004-M:L13], and the thing here was sweet in the most literal sense available: a bark whose entire value is its taste and its smell, about two-thirds to four-fifths of whose oil is the one aldehyde that carries the smell. It attaches to a pleasing or to a neutral object and never comes with displeasure [C004-P:L41] [C004-M:L15], which is why this film has no villain in it and is not permitted one. And the sense-sphere world the count is a count of [C004-P:L25] is not a trap: twenty-four of the fifty-four are classed beautiful [C004-P:L27], so the film cannot end on a warning about appetite, and the last beat says so.

C032 supplies the other half of the object, and it is the half the title rests on. This digest's subject is the flavour of an object and feeling as the bare tasting of it, present in every mind because every mind takes an object [C032-P:L41] [C032-P:L43], going three ways with no fourth [C032-M:L5], with sixty-two kinds of mind counted glad and fifty-five flat [C032-M:L9] [C032-M:L13]. A wall built round a flavour is therefore not a metaphor here, it is the literal description of the site, and the warehouse inside the rampart is where the flavour was kept at temperature. The same digest also carries the film's one honest way of handling what the record does not contain. It separates open suffering — violence and confinement that anyone can see — from concealed suffering, which cannot be known unless somebody asks [C032-P:L119]. The obligation, the quotas, the registers and the punishments are all in the Company's own papers; nothing written by the people under the obligation was found in researching this film. That is a statement about an archive, not a verdict on anybody, and it is the sources' own distinction rather than an editorial one, which is exactly why it is safe to say.
what_is_certain: A walled town stands on a rock headland closing the west side of a bay on the island's south coast. It is inhabited, it is a declared World Heritage property, and the rampart circuit can be walked.

The Portuguese landed on this coast in 1505 and chose the place as a permanent post in 1588, after an attack by Rajasinha I of Sitawaka. What they built was described as a work of palm trees and mud called Santa Cruz, later extended with a watchtower, three bastions and a fortalice guarding the harbour.

The Dutch East India Company took the place from the Portuguese in 1640, in alliance with Rajasinha II of Kandy, under Commodore Willem Jacobszoon Coster; the Portuguese captain was Lourenço Ferreira de Brito. Modern accounts put the assault at 8–13 March 1640, with the surrender on 13 March.

From 1640 the Company's Ceylon administration was seated here, until Colombo was taken from the Portuguese in 1656. After that the capital was Colombo and this became one of two commandements under the governor there, while remaining the island's principal port.

The standing fortifications are Dutch and post-date the capture. The Company judged the Portuguese earthworks unsafe and walled the peninsula; the main run of the walls is dated to 1663 and the sea wall was completed in 1729.

The oldest gate was completed in 1669. Its inner (town) face carries the VOC coat of arms, two lions holding a monogram with a cockerel above it and the date ANNO MDCLXIX; its outer (harbour) face carries the British royal arms of George III, a crown between a lion and a unicorn with the motto Dieu et mon droit. The British moved the VOC emblem to the inside when they took the fort and put their own arms on the seaward face.

A two-storey warehouse of 1671 stands above that gate and, unusually for this company's fortifications, part of the building is embodied in the thickness of the rampart. Cinnamon, cardamom and cloves were kept in the cool basement; gems, pearls, silk, porcelain and ivory in the dry rooms above. The building is now the National Maritime Museum, opened to the public on 9 May 1992.

The usual list names fourteen bastions: Sun, Moon, Star, Zwart, Akersloot, Aurora, Point Utrecht, Triton, Neptune, Clippenburg, Flagrock, Aeolus, Fishmark and Commandment. An eighteenth-century engraved plan held in the Dutch archive keys the Sun, Moon, Star, Aeolus and Triton works and also a work called die Katz.
Cinnamon was the Company's principal commodity on the island and the reason for its presence on this coast.
Before European rule, cinnamon extraction was carried out through rajakariya, the system of unpaid labour owed to the monarchy and aristocracy.

Under colonial rule the extraction and supply of cinnamon was organised through a department known as the Mahabadda, placed under a Company officer called the captain of cinnamon, which took delivery of fixed quantities without payment from men of the Salagama caste as an obligatory hereditary caste service. The Dutch kept registers of the men, punished absence and shortfall, and legislated that marriage into another caste did not release a man from the obligation.

A nineteenth-century compilation (John Ferguson, drawing on earlier accounts) records that the Dutch limited the number of plants and destroyed the excess, that prepared cinnamon was frequently thrown into the sea or burnt, and that on 10 June 1760 an enormous quantity was destroyed near the Admiralty at Amsterdam, valued at eight millions of livres, with an equal quantity burnt the following day.
The Company turned from wild cinnamon to cultivation from about 1769–1770, under Governor Iman Willem Falck, with a large plantation laid out at Maradana by Cornelis de Cock.
The British took the fort on 23 February 1796. The cinnamon monopoly passed to the English East India Company and was abolished in 1833 or 1834.

The first lighthouse was built by the British in 1848, a cast-iron tower designed by Alexander Gordon and made by Robinson of Pimlico. A new main gate was cut through the north wall in 1873 and a clock tower was erected for Queen Victoria's jubilee in 1883.
The harbour's primacy ended with the artificial harbour built at Colombo from 1873; by December 1882 the P&O mail steamers had moved their base from here to Colombo.

The property was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1988 as the Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications, under criterion (iv), as an urban ensemble illustrating the interaction of European architecture and South Asian traditions from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries.

People have lived inside the walls continuously since the colonial period and more than half of the residents are recorded as Moors. Research by Uditha Jinadasa of Leiden University, reported in March 2020, gives the resident population as 2,703 in 1988 and 1,068 at the time of the study; residential buildings fell from 72 per cent in 1992 to 32 per cent in 2016 while commercial buildings rose from 17 per cent to 35 per cent; 66 per cent of facades had been altered since 1988; and 16 per cent of the real estate was in foreign hands in 2016.

The warehouse building survived the tsunami of 26 December 2004; the adjoining maritime archaeology unit did not and its exhibitions were flood-damaged. This is recorded here as a fact about the site and is excluded from every beat of the film.
what_is_disputed: The date of the first fortification on the headland. One account dates the Zwart Bastion, the Black Fort, to 1520; another dates a Franciscan chapel to 1541; the standard account has the Portuguese choosing the place as a permanent post only in 1588. None of these is reconciled in the sources consulted and the film states only that the Portuguese work was slight and of earth and palisade.

The date of the Dutch capture. Modern accounts give 8–13 March 1640. The Dutch national archive's own caption on the contemporary print of the event states that the conquest took place on 9 February 1640. No explanation for the difference — calendar, a preliminary action, or simple error — was established. The film says March 1640 and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.

The size of the 1640 expedition and its casualties. One account gives some 2,500 men under Coster; another gives 3,350 European troops with unnumbered sailors, Bandanese and Malay troops, 24 ships and at least 27 shallops. Dutch dead are given as 450 European troops in one place and as high as 1,350 in another. Nothing is averaged and no figure is used in the voice.

When Galle ceased to be the Company's Ceylon capital. The Atlas of Mutual Heritage and several accounts give 1656, the year Colombo was taken; other pages give 1658, the year the Portuguese were finally expelled. The brief's own note that this was 'the VOC's principal stronghold' is not supportable as a general statement: it was the administrative centre for about sixteen years and the principal port thereafter, under a governor seated elsewhere.

The date the Dutch fortifications were built. 1649 onwards, 1663 for the main run of the walls, and 1667 for a general fortifying and enlargement all appear; 1669 for the oldest gate and 1729 for the sea wall are consistent across sources.

The enclosed area. 52 hectares (130 acres) is repeated almost everywhere, including on tourism and heritage pages, and no official Department of Archaeology or World Heritage nomination figure was located to stand behind it. One Wikipedia article gives 36 hectares (89 acres) and calls the fort hexagonal, which the plan is not. The rampart circuit is described as over 2.5 km, from a visitor review rather than a survey. No figure is spoken in the voice.

The number of bastions. Fourteen is the standard list, but an eighteenth-century plan in the Dutch archive keys a work, die Katz, that is not on it, and half-bastions are counted inconsistently between accounts.

Every date attached to the lighthouse. The fire that destroyed the 1848 tower is given as 1934 by one source and as July 1936 by another; the present tower is dated 1938, 1939 and 1940 across three sources; its height is given as 18 m, 24 m, 26 m, 26.5 m and 92 ft; the old tower's site is given as the Flagrock bastion by one source and Point Utrecht by another; and the distance between old and new sites as 100 m and as 200 m. None of this is used in the voice and the lighthouse appears only as an object in frame.

Who made the cinnamon obligation caste-bound, and when. One account dates the Mahabadda's operation from 1597 and states that the Portuguese already used the same caste as cinnamon planters paying cinnamon as a tax; the Salagama Wikipedia article cites the Heladiva Bamunuwatha chronicle for the caste being ordered to peel cinnamon in the reign of Sapumal Kumaraya, 1447–1480, and describes the caste as formerly weavers of South Indian origin; and a 2024 scholarly essay states that it was the Dutch who changed the social division of labour by segregating the role and assigning it to that caste, with the department taking over extraction and supply later. The brief's own note that the peelers were 'a caste-bound workforce under the Dutch' is therefore too simple: the Dutch registered, quota'd and punished it, but the record does not establish that they invented it. What is not in dispute is the machinery, and the film states only that.

The punishments. Press coverage of Dr Dilhani Dissanayake's La Trobe doctoral research reports that peelers had their ears cut off, were confined in chains, and were whipped and branded. Other pages state that private dealing in cinnamon was punishable by death and that destroying plants carried the death penalty in one locality and whipping elsewhere. The thesis itself was not read, and no ordinance or plakkaat text was checked against a scholarly edition in this research. The severity of the regime is well supported in outline; the specific punishments and their legal form are not verified here.

The peelers' own record. No first-person account by anyone under the obligation was located in this research. That is a finding about what was searched, not a claim that none exists, and the film's line is worded as a statement about the archive rather than about the people.

The export figures. 8,000 to 10,000 bales a year, an income of 2.5 million guilders a year, and a million bales shipped over the whole period are repeated online, and all of them trace to a single unattributed museum article that also dates the capture of Galle to 1638 and the force to 2,000 men. A scholarly summary of Wagenaar's Cinnamon and Elephants gives only 'hundreds of thousands of pounds annually'. No figure is used.

The 1760 destruction at Amsterdam. The specific claim — 10 June 1760, an enormous quantity near the Admiralty, eight millions of livres, as much again the next day — comes from Ferguson's Ceylon in 1893, reproducing an earlier account, and was not traced to an archival source. It is attributed in the voice to the record rather than asserted as verified, and the general practice of destroying stock to hold the price is corroborated separately.
The date cultivation began. About 1770 in Ferguson, 1769 for Falck's seed-raising at Grandpass, and 1789 for de Cock laying out the Maradana garden on Falck's orders. Not reconciled.
The abolition of the monopoly. 1833 and 1834 both appear. Rajakariya is separately reported as abolished in 1832.

The name. Gimhathiththa is reported as the older name and glossed as the port near the Gin river; the modern name is derived variously from Sinhala gala, meaning rock or a place where cattle are herded, and from Portuguese galo, a rooster, the latter supported by the cockerel over the Company's arms on the gate but also plainly capable of having produced that cockerel rather than the reverse. Sir James Emerson Tennent identified the place with the biblical Tarshish. None of this is settled and none of it is in the voice.

The claim, repeated on commercial spice pages, that the island's cinnamon could be smelled eight leagues out to sea when the wind blew off the land. No early modern text was located for it and it is not used.

what_to_film: The foot of the rampart from outside, walked, in overhead sun: coral and granite courses, salt bloom, the sea glaring beyond. Ground level only; this film opens on a wall and not on an aerial.
A continuous walk along the rampart top with the circuit running away in both directions, the bastion angles turning the line, the town's roofs inside and open water outside.

The warehouse from outside, showing that the two-storey building is inside the thickness of the rampart and that the gate is driven through the middle of it. This shot is the film's whole argument in one frame and the schedule is built round getting it.
The vaulted interiors of that warehouse: thick walls, bare floors, the difference in the air at the doorway. Subject to the conserving authority, and the film has no middle without it.

The two faces of the gate arch, matched in lens and distance so that they cut against each other: the harbour side with the crown, lion and unicorn, and the town side with the two lions, the monogram, the cockerel and ANNO MDCLXIX.
The gate passage from inside, static and long, as the full depth of the wall: a dark tunnel with white light at the far end and traffic crossing it in silhouette.
The batter of a bastion from directly below in vertical sun, with heat shimmer off the coral and nothing moving in frame.
The lighthouse on the seaward bastion in flat glare, and past it the empty roadstead; then the jubilee clock tower on the landward wall.

The streets at walking pace: the grid, shutters, salt-marked plaster, an animal in a crossroads, a minaret and a church tower over the roofline, the sea at the end of a street. People only as they pass; nobody held, nobody followed, no interiors of houses.

An eighteenth-century engraved plan of the fort with its lettered bastion key, filmed as a document, for beat 5. The Dutch archival plans are the right kind and are reproducible; the shot is of a print, not of the site.
suggested_location.access: Inside the district town, at the seaward end, reached on public roads and entered through either the 1669 gate on the harbour side or the 1873 main gate on the north wall. The streets are public, the rampart circuit is walkable self-guided in daylight, and there is no ticket for the town itself. Three conditions matter more than the road. It is a declared World Heritage property and an archaeological reserve, so filming on the ramparts and the standing fabric is a matter for the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund rather than a visitor permission. The warehouse interior, which the film depends on, is a state museum with its own conditions and hours. And it is somebody's street: a residential grid where the number of residents has fallen sharply and where the people who remain are heavily photographed, so the terms on which the streets are filmed have to be settled on the ground before anything is scheduled. Drone should be treated as requiring specific clearance over a World Heritage property, a working harbour and an inhabited town, and the film is designed to need none.
suggested_location.best_time: The dry months on this coast, roughly December to March, and within the day the hard hours either side of noon — deliberately the opposite of how this place is normally photographed. High sun bleaches the coral, flattens the modelling in the wall and makes the gate passage read as a hole; it is also what keeps the film off the sunset rampart image that every visitor makes. The vaulted interiors want the middle of the day for the largest possible difference in the doorway. A second slot is worth planning for weather rather than light: a rough sea on the seaward bastions, and a calm one for the circuit.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 26 September 2026. No access, permission, museum condition, drone clearance or street-level arrangement has been verified, and nothing was checked on the ground or against a printed edition or an archival document. Coordinates are the walled town's centre point as given for the fort and were not surveyed. Four things in the brief's own row note were corrected by this research and are recorded in what_is_disputed rather than carried as fact. First, 'the VOC's principal stronghold' is too strong: the Company's Ceylon administration sat here only from 1640 until Colombo was taken in 1656 (some sources say 1658), after which this was one of two commandements under a governor seated elsewhere, though it remained the island's principal port until the 1870s. Second, 'the fort that stands' is not the fort that was captured in 1640: the main walls date to 1663, the oldest gate to 1669, the warehouse above it to 1671 and the sea wall to 1729, so the standing circuit is a generation and more later than the capture, and the date of the Dutch rebuilding is itself given variously as 1649 onwards, 1663 and 1667. Third, the caste-bound workforce was not simply created by the Dutch: pre-European extraction ran on rajakariya, one account dates the cinnamon department to 1597 in the Portuguese period and says the Portuguese already took cinnamon as a tax from the same caste, a Sinhala chronicle is cited for an assignment in the fifteenth century, and a 2024 scholarly essay credits the Dutch with segregating and assigning the role — so the sources genuinely disagree, and the film states only the machinery, which they do not dispute. Fourth, the British takeover is datable precisely to 23 February 1796, a week after Colombo. Beyond the row, the pattern the project keeps finding held again. The 52-hectare area, the fourteen bastions and the 2.5 km circuit are repeated everywhere and could not be traced to an official nomination or survey, and one Wikipedia article gives 36 hectares and calls the plan hexagonal. Every date and dimension attached to the lighthouse conflicts across three sources, including two different bastions for the old tower's site. The export figures most often quoted — 8,000 to 10,000 bales a year, 2.5 million guilders a year, a million bales in total — all trace to a single unattributed museum web article which also dates the capture to 1638 and the force to 2,000 men, and they are not used. The Dutch national archive's own caption on the contemporary print of the capture dates it to 9 February 1640 against the modern 8–13 March, which is recorded and not resolved. The 1760 destruction at Amsterdam comes from Ferguson's Ceylon in 1893 reproducing an older account and is attributed as such in the voice. The reported punishments of the peelers come from press coverage of Dr Dilhani Dissanayake's La Trobe doctorate; the thesis was not read and no ordinance text was checked. No first-person record by anyone under the cinnamon obligation was found, which is stated in the film as a fact about the archive rather than about the people. The claim that the island's cinnamon could be smelled eight leagues out to sea appears only on commercial spice pages with no attribution and is not used. Nine reference images were located through the Commons search API and every one was confirmed to exist through action=query&titles= before its URL was written; all nine are of this site or of an archival plan of it, and each caption says what it is. The UNESCO record at whc.unesco.org/en/list/451 returned HTTP 403 and could not be fetched directly; the inscription year, criterion and name are taken from secondary pages quoting it and the property area could not be confirmed there.

unknowns: No access, permission or contact has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
Whether the interior of the warehouse built into the rampart can be filmed at all, and on what terms, is the single thing the film depends on and it is unverified.
Whether both faces of the gate arch can be filmed cleanly, given the traffic through it and any scaffolding or conservation work in progress, has not been checked.

The Department of Archaeology and Central Cultural Fund conditions for filming on a World Heritage property, and whether they come with framing requirements the film could not honestly accept, are unknown.
Drone rules over a World Heritage property, a working harbour and an inhabited town are unverified; the film is designed not to need one.

How the streets can be filmed without residents becoming subjects, in a small residential grid where the population is falling and the place is heavily photographed, has not been worked out on the ground.
Whether a reproducible archival plan of the fort can be filmed as a document, and under what rights, has not been established.

Whether the enclosed area, the rampart length and the bastion count can be established from an official survey rather than from repetition is unresolved, and no figure is spoken in the film until it is.

Whether any first-person record by a person subject to the cinnamon obligation survives in the Dutch or British archives is unknown; this research found none and the film's line is worded accordingly.
